problem.title: Design a URL Shortener
problem.prompt: Design a URL shortening service similar to bit.ly or TinyURL. Users submit a long URL and receive a short alias (e.g., https://short.ly/aB3xY). When a user visits the short URL, the service redirects them to the original. The service must handle high read traffic, provide low-latency redirects, and allow optional analytics per short URL.
requirements: Given a long URL, generate a unique short alias and return it to the user.
Given a short alias, resolve and redirect to the original URL with low latency.
Short aliases must be unique and collision-resistant.
Optionally support custom aliases chosen by the user.
Optionally record click count and basic analytics per short URL.
Short URLs should not expire by default; expiry is an optional configuration.
constraints: Write volume: ~100 million new URLs per day (assume 100:1 read-to-write ratio).
Redirect p99 latency target: under 10 ms.
Alias length: 7 characters (default) using [a-z, A-Z, 0-9] — 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion combinations.
Data retention: indefinite unless expiry is explicitly set.
Assume globally distributed read traffic, writes concentrated in a few regions.

stages.learnerPrompt: Before designing, clarify the problem scope. What are the core functional requirements? What constraints and scale assumptions define the design space? Identify what is given, what you must assume, and what is explicitly out of scope.

referenceMaterial.summary: Core requirements: generate short alias → store mapping → resolve + redirect. Key constraints: 100M writes/day ≈ 1,160 writes/sec; 100:1 read ratio ≈ 116,000 reads/sec; 62^7 alias space; p99 redirect < 10 ms. Out of scope for base design: per-user authentication, abuse prevention, real-time analytics dashboards.
tradeOffs: Global read traffic favors edge caching or a distributed KV store over a single relational DB.
Custom aliases introduce collision risk and require reservation logic separate from the ID generation path.

stages.learnerPrompt: Sketch your initial design. How would you generate short aliases? Where do you store the long-to-short mapping? How do you handle redirects at scale? Write your approach before revealing the reference solution.
Review the reference architecture. Compare it to your approach — note where they align and where they differ.

referenceMaterial.summary: Two-tier architecture: an ID generation service produces 7-character Base-62 aliases; a write path stores the mapping (shortId → longUrl, metadata) in a distributed KV store (e.g., DynamoDB or Cassandra); a read path resolves aliases via an in-memory cache (Redis) in front of the KV store and returns an HTTP 301/302 redirect.
approachSteps: 1. Client submits POST /shorten with the long URL.
2. API layer validates and rate-limits the request.
3. ID Generator creates a unique 7-char Base-62 alias (using a counter with Base-62 encoding or a hash-then-truncate strategy).
4. Write the mapping {shortId → longUrl, createdAt, userId?} to the KV store. Check uniqueness before committing.
5. Return the full short URL (https://short.ly/{alias}) to the client.
6. For redirect: client GET /alias → API checks Redis cache → on miss, reads KV store → returns 301 (permanent) or 302 (trackable) redirect.
7. Cache the mapping in Redis on first read (TTL-based). Hot URLs stay in cache indefinitely under TTL.
referenceMaterial.diagramDescription: Client → API Gateway → ID Generator (stateless) → KV Store (write); Client → CDN/Edge → Redis Cache → KV Store (read) → HTTP 3xx Redirect.
alternatives: Hash-then-truncate (MD5/SHA256 of long URL, take first 7 chars): simpler but collision-prone; requires collision retry loop.
Centralized counter + Base-62 encode: globally unique but single-node bottleneck; mitigated with distributed counter partitioning.
UUID-based: collision-free but 36-char aliases — impractical for short links.
Geographically distributed counter ranges (Twitter Snowflake-style): eliminates bottleneck at cost of coordination overhead.

stages.learnerPrompt: Why 301 vs 302 redirect? Why Base-62 over UUID? What are the ID generation trade-offs? Walk through each key design decision and explain what it optimizes for.

tradeOffs: 301 (Permanent): Browser caches the redirect, reducing repeat load on the service. Cost: no click analytics on cached requests. Use when analytics are not needed.
302 (Temporary/Found): Every visit hits the service, enabling click counting. Cost: higher server load for popular links. Use when analytics are required.
Base-62 vs hash: Base-62 counter gives monotonically increasing, collision-free IDs at the cost of a coordination step. Hash-truncate is simpler but requires a collision retry mechanism.
Redis as redirect cache: Cold start adds one KV read per alias. Warm state handles virtually all read traffic without touching the persistent store — critical for the p99 < 10 ms target.
Custom aliases: Require a separate namespace to avoid collisions with generated IDs. Store in the same KV with a reserved prefix or a separate index.
alternatives: Skip caching (Redis) and read from KV directly: feasible for DynamoDB with sub-ms reads in the same region, but adds cross-region latency. Cache is recommended for global traffic.
Relational DB (Postgres) instead of KV: simpler query model and transactional custom-alias uniqueness checks. Bottleneck at 116,000 reads/sec requires read replicas + aggressive caching.

stages.learnerPrompt: What happens when a single short URL receives millions of hits in minutes (viral link)? How does your design handle ID exhaustion, cache failure, and regional outages?

referenceMaterial.summary: Handling hot links, exhaustion, and failure modes.
failureModes: Hot/viral link: Single alias generates millions of cache reads. Redis handles this as a single key — but if that key evicts or Redis restarts, the KV store absorbs a thundering herd. Mitigation: never evict hot keys (LFU eviction policy + keep TTL long for popular links); use probabilistic early refresh.
ID space exhaustion: 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion — at 100M/day it takes ~95 years. Non-issue for MVP. Future: extend alias length to 8 chars (62^8 ≈ 218 trillion).

ID generator failure: If using a centralized counter, a single-node failure stops ID generation. Mitigation: replicate the counter with leader election (Zookeeper/etcd) or switch to a distributed range-based scheme.

Cache failure (Redis down): All redirects fall back to KV reads. At 116K reads/sec this can overwhelm KV. Mitigation: circuit breaker on the cache client; read replicas on the KV store; multi-layer edge cache (CDN) for the most popular links.

Regional outage: Cross-region replication of the KV store with eventual consistency. Reads from the nearest region. Writes: accept last-write-wins for duplicate short alias creation across regions (acceptable given the collision probability is extremely low).

stages.learnerPrompt: Changed constraint: the product team now requires real-time click analytics — total clicks, unique visitors (by IP hash), and referrer breakdown — accessible within 5 seconds of a click. How does this change your design? What new components do you introduce and what trade-offs arise?

referenceMaterial.summary: Adding real-time analytics: event streaming path
approachSteps: 1. On each redirect request, publish a lightweight click event (shortId, timestamp, ipHash, referrer) to a Kafka topic asynchronously — do NOT block the redirect path.
2. A Flink or Kafka Streams job aggregates events over 5-second tumbling windows and writes counts to a time-series store (ClickHouse, DynamoDB with TTL, or Redis sorted sets).
3. An Analytics API reads from the aggregated store and serves dashboards.
4. To track unique visitors without storing PII, use HyperLogLog (Redis) for approximate cardinality — accurate to within 1% error.
tradeOffs: Async event emission on the redirect path: keeps redirect latency unaffected but risks losing click events if Kafka is unavailable. Accept at-least-once delivery with deduplication downstream.
Real-time window vs batch: 5-second windows require streaming infrastructure. Hourly batch (simpler) would not meet the requirement.
HyperLogLog for unique visitors: ~1% error is acceptable for analytics; exact counts require storing user identifiers, raising privacy concerns.
